catalog_quote: Efutu uses tone to distinguish lexical items, as in the minimal pairs in (3-19). ... Four tone patterns were identified in the data from my fieldwork. They may be characterised as: (i) High tone , (ii) Low tone , (iii) Falling tone and (iv) Downstep-high tone (!). ... High tone and Low tone may be said to be basic in Efutu as they may occur independently in words. Unlike High and Low tone, Downstep-high and Falling appear to be secondary; they usually do not occur independently. ... Downstep-high tone usually occurs after High tone, whereas Falling tone may occur after High or Low tone. From the data, Downstep-high and Falling tone seem to occur in word-final position while High and Low tone tend to have wider distributions. ... Tone has both lexical and grammatical functions in Efutu. Lexically, meaning of words is distinguished based on tone differentiation, as in (3-19). Gr…
sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Awutu: Lomotey 2014, 'The prosodic realization of focus in Awutu', an unpublished ACAL 45 conference paper (Glottolog 632249, harvested from the LangSci 121 bibliography). It concerns focus/sentence prosody, not word stress. The paper text could not be found anywhere open (no DOI; ACAL 45 site suspended; program booklet not archived; Internet Archive offline; Its only published trace, read and saved, is Cahill 2017 (LangSci 121, ch. 2, p. 26): 'In Awutu (Lomotey 2014), a deliberate attempt to have speakers focus on one part of a sentence produced almost no pitch variation.' The author's companion ASA abstract (Lomotey 2013, JASA 134: 4246, Crossref record saved) states first-hand that Awutu uses F0 'to signal lexical tone', not prominence. Both are consistent with, and neither refines or contradicts, the catalog's 'tonal' coding resting on Agyeman 2016; no word-stress statement for Awutu was found. Acquisition priority for the 2014 paper: low.

new_statements.quote: Besides, while English uses fundamental frequency in its intonation system, to indicate prominence in syllables and in phrases, and to signal differences in sentence intonation, Awutu uses it to signal lexical tone, a common phenomenon of tone languages. The present study investigates the effect of transfer of some prosodic features of Awutu, a language of Ghana, on English. To achieve this, 10 speakers of Awutu who are non-native speakers of English were asked to read narrow and broad focus statements and questions in both Awutu and English.
new_statements.citation: Lomotey, Charlotte F. 2013. Does first language prosodic transfer affect second language prosody? Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 134(5, Suppl.): 4246 (ASA meeting abstract). doi:10.1121/1.4831620
new_statements.reading: A first-hand, instrumentally based (CSL, F0) statement by the one phonetician who has worked on Awutu prosody: Awutu is a lexical tone language in which F0 carries tone, not syllable/phrase prominence; no word-stress or accent-placement rule is stated. This is a tone-language classification, not a stress statement, and it comes from a meeting abstract (no full paper found); it is consistent with the catalog's 'tonal' coding but adds no stress rule.

sources.quote: 'Efutu is a tone language. Tone is used to distinguish between two otherwise similar words, Obeng (2008). ... Efutu has two level tones namely high and low. Tone in Efutu is phonemic and Efutu only makes use of intonation in polar questions.' Polar questions marked by an extra low tone docking on the final syllable. No word-stress rule anywhere; the only 'stress' token (p. 10) is Dixon's generic phonological-word criterion, illustrated for Efutu with tone minimal pairs only.

sources.quote: Cruttenden (1997: 73) notes that tone languages are less likely to use intonation as a means of focus than non-tone languages, and several recent studies affirm this. In Awutu (Lomotey 2014), a deliberate attempt to have speakers focus on one part of a sentence produced almost no pitch variation.
